I always try to finish a book, as I think there is something to be learned even from what initially appears to be a 'bad' book. 
It took me almost 18-months to finish reading The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich. It was 1300 pages densely filled with so many facts about a horrific time in history that I constantly needed to take a break for a week or more before I could pick it up again. In the end, I was glad that I finished reading it as the book gave me a different perspective not only about the events surrounding WWII but about current political events, as well. 
However, I will not continue reading a book if it contains violence for shock value. I threw in the towel after 2 chapters of a gothic novel which opened with a detailed description of mutilated dead cats that continued into the 2nd chapter. There is enough violence in the world and in the news-I don't need more in the books I read.

But as a social scientist, I'm amazed to be living through a seismic technological change transforming human social life, similar to what happened around 12K years ago with the advent of farming and animal domestication. 

In a seeming instant, human social life transformed from small, mostly egalitarian, nomadic foraging bands to large, highly stratified, settled towns and cities where ruling classes lived well, serviced by skilled artisans and supported by peasant labor. The ruling classes of course had to employ militias to suppress the "expendables" who inevitably emerge in a society where few have everything and most have little or nothing (check out the work of Gerhard Lenski, nicely summarized in Häkkinen, S. (2016). Poverty in the first-century Galilee. HTS Teologiese Studies Theological Studies, 72(4). https://doi.org/10.4102/hts.v72i4.3398). 

Hope my family (artisan class) quickly gets enough money to grab the bottom rung of the ruling class and hang on for dear life!

PS: I quickly wrote the above verbiage without the help of AI - except for 1) correcting my spelling of "expendable" and 2) looking up the Häkkinen reference. Hmmm, does that count as AI use? Do tell...

Not mentioned in this piece is the incredibly uneven training and education of therapists, counselors, and mental health "professionals."  

I think a good, if controversial, example is provided by the "gender medicine" domain, which was largely unregulated, populated by many untrained and under-trained clinicians, too often guided by ideology rather than by empirical evidence and common sense, and which ultimately led to serious ethical and professional abuses.

comments.name: James K.
comments.body:
A very fine history of psychotherapy theory and practice. And especially for debunking the flawed supposition that CBT alone is superior because it is friendly to scientific study investigation. (When Prozac was going off-patent, the pharmaceutical company sought to extend it by finding a new use for it:  treating depression in dogs. one must wonder - what was the variable used in studies to represent the level of depression - tail wags per minute?)
The problem with your hopes with Predictive Processing Theory is the same one that has dogged the rise of neuroscience - all of the important and useful aspects of your model are theory, rather than demonstrated fact. And neuroscience is especially complicit in blurring the line between theory and fact.Neuroscience researcher David Eagleman typifies this 'slight of hand' confabulation: One of his studies show that people whose names are similar to the word dentist (Donna, Dennis, etc.) disproportionately choose dentistry as a vocation. That's a fact. He goes on to say they do so because of the narcissism of having one's name associated with a prestigious occupation. That's pure, unsubstantiated theory. 
Neuroscience is rife with attributions of various patterns of brain activity as signifiers of important behavioral consequences - presented as fact, rather than theoretical suppositions. Strip current neuroscience of its theoretical suppositions, and what is left is mostly a much less utilitarian collection of 'stupid human tricks'

comments.name: Nicole.dubus
comments.body: While the author makes a thoughtful analysis of therapy's effectiveness, he relies on his perspective heavily, leaving out elements that are equally as important. I am a licensed clinical social worker, and we practice differently than psychoanalists. We see the inner worlds of individuals inextricably woven with their environments. Yes, childhood experiences pave pathways that are foundational to how we perceive the world. And so too does poverty, oppression, abuse, and our climate crisis. Society's institutions shape our beliefs in ourselves, others, and inform how we think, feel, and behave. A clinican can't isolate one factor as the cause of "disorder", a term the DSM5 uses to describe a client's experience. The very term reveals its bias. Whose disorder? Which leads to "what causes this disorder?" "What fixes it?" In social work, you can not separate out the individual from society. We live within systems that enhance and burden us. If I am physically abused and the police and legal system don't believe me, how helpful is it to challenge my fears if the systems meant to protect instead side with the abuser? Social work seeks to understand the experiences of the individual and address unjust institutions within society. Neurobiology has increased our understanding of our experience; but by focusing soley on this, we place the burden of wellbeing on the shoulders of those most vulnerable. To be helpful, we must also work toward the well-being of society and social justice.

I'd love to see a comparably oriented review of the discourse from someone who was not as steeped in the online section of discourse.

Nolan's Odyssey, while full of adaptive changes good and bad, does an excellent job of steering the narrative context towards the conflicts we see reflected in the world today. As a result, I have had and observed numerous vigorous conversations among adults discussing what they were drawn to, what they didn't understand, and what resonated. This is the type of 'monocultural' media  engagement for which I and others are nostalgic.

That being said, Nolan's Odyssey is a titanic achievement in visual storytelling and mythical realism while also being an exception of success that proves the rule of the industry's declining market share. The amount of money that is required to make a movie at this scale, shot mostly on location, and market it appropriately is staggering and requires the type of constellatory alignment of circumstances that cannot be manufactured. 

Movies more broadly cannot subsist on the externalities of the tentpole movies that are driving the congratulatory industry media binge, but apparently opinion pieces can.

comments.body:
The Odyssey is about one man’s struggles and easier to relate to than the Iliad where everyone behaves badly. There are heroes, but no consistent good guys and bad buys. UFC has nothing on the one-on-one combat in the Iliad. If anything, the Odyssey demonstrates the value of having a GPS and a devoted trusted following. The Odyssey may have had some inspirational part is the disasters in Voltaire’s Candide, Don Quixote, and other picaresque tales.  Odysseus is no more heroic than Achilles, but he is indefatigable like Ahab chasing Moby Dick. He is the ET of Greek mythology, just wanting to go home. 

So, why does it resonate today?  What we are seeing is hype heaped upon hype, justified by reading into the famous tale of travels and travails, what may not have been intended. This was a tale for Greek minstrels to sing, It as entertainment then, and it is entertainment now. In a year or two, the IMAX film may become like the pet rocks and the hula hoops, just a contagions must-see. 

But Homer(s) will live in through the great pair of stories, one that ends in tragedy (pile on other tragedies) which begins the fateful journey through danger and demons, magic and mystery, to rejoin his faithful wife. It is the sequel to the Iliad focused on a man and his crew. Maybe someday a film maker will reunite this two tales into an all day film like Wagner’s Götterdämmerung or Robert Wilson’s and Phillip Glass’s Einstein on the Beach. The event overshadows the story.

One important lesson that comes from Putnam's work is that none of this was led by the state and government institutions. Government institutions and the state, broadly conceived, only responded to changes in the broader society.

Putnam's chapters on the backlash against improving racial equality and gender relations demands more investigation. Why did this dramatic reversal take shape at the end of the 1960s and continue until the present? As I was born in 1970,  this is a sobering question, because all I have seen my entire life has been decline. 

Part of this exists in the fundamental values that used to unite Americans: traditional liberalism. Written into our Constitution, these values served us very well up to the 1960s, but then we turned on them, although we did not appreciate what we were doing at the time. 

The challenges to traditional liberalism now come equally from the left and the right, from the Democratic Party and the Republican Party.

I will suggest three books for further reading.
1) Francis Fukuyama, "Liberalism and Its Discontents."
2) Edmund Fawcett, "Liberalism: The life of an Idea."
3) Adrian Wooldridge, "The Revolutionary Center."

Merit. Equality. The dignity of the individual. Universalism. Belief in progress, but not revolution.

The article's fundamental flaw lies in completely reversing cause and effect. It frames public skepticism, independent media, and alternative networks as a defect of ordinary citizens getting "tricked" by algorithms or cell phones. But people didn't abandon traditional gatekeepers on a whim. Trust in legacy media, political leadership, and civic institutions didn't plummet because of podcasts or headphones; it collapsed because those institutions repeatedly broke their promise of neutrality, delivered failed policies, and refused to hold themselves accountable.

Invoking Hannah Arendt and Robert Putnam to equate decentralized news consumption with "toxic ideologies" or a precursor to totalitarianism is a classic sleight of hand. Decentralization isn't a disease that infected a healthy public—it is the direct, rational public response to institutional failure. Using The New York Times masthead to validate personal nostalgia for an era of top-down narrative control doesn't make it journalism. It simply demonstrates why millions of readers stopped trusting legacy media in the first place

Private credit’s growing strain cannot be separated from the PE ecosystem that feeds many of its borrowers. The model can work when acquisition debt is paired with real operational improvement. But its more sinister version relies on high leverage, dividend recaps, fee extraction, asset sales, and “adjusted” earnings. Leaving an operating company with less resilience and a larger debt burden. Private credit has increasingly financed that structure.

The concern is not that every PE-backed company is being “asset stripped,” nor that retail investors alone will bear losses. Sponsors can lose equity and lenders can take real impairments. But the risk transfer is problematic - opaque loans are valued largely by managers, difficult restructurings can be deferred through amendments or payment-in-kind interest, and non-traded BDCs offer retail investors limited liquidity right about the time they want out.

The data points suggest the system is being tested while the broader economy is still reasonably stable. If borrowers are already struggling before a serious downturn, a recession could turn gradual markdowns into correlated defaults, refinancing shortfalls, redemption gates, and sharper losses.

PE and PC  are not inherently unsustainable. However the greed and inevitable incentive to "play games" increases the risk we go.  Their real test is whether their underwriting, valuations, and liquidity  promises survive the coming contraction.

A few years ago, I visited the mammoth dig site in Rapid City SD. I was wearing a Great Gatsby T-shirt my wife bought me as a souvenir for our trip to Portland’s Powell’s Books and I browsed the T-shirts in the gift shop for a souvenir of our somewhat harrowing trip to Rapid City the week before Sturgis officially begins. A woman—from her manner clearly bristling with degrees—approached me to ask why I wore the T-shirt and I simply replied it is my favorite novel. (I have read it a dozen times or more.) She promptly attacked the novel as dreadful and by implication questioned my morality, my intelligence and status as a human being.
Please do not judge what I read. It really is none of your business. The prizes and such as boring and meaningless. Even the Nobel Prize brilliantly avoided giving both Tolstoy and Borges the big bucks. 
Academics in general have awful taste. The canon is not perpetuated believe it or not by academics. It is perpetuated by people like me who just like to read which is why today oddities like Philip K. Dick and Maus have a better chance of surviving than almost any Booker Prize awardee.

The US has depleted supplies of our very expensive munitions so deeply that it simply isn't possible to commit to large additional offensive operations.  Nor are there sufficient interceptors of various types to adequately defend US and allied sites in the Gulf.  We don't have an adequate military industrial capacity to replenish those stocks faster than several years — at best.

Even if enough weapons were available, there is no scenario in which the US could cripple Iran's offensive capabilities before Tehran destroyed the energy and potable water infrastructure of the Gulf Arab states.  It would take many years for the industry to recover, if it ever could.  In the meantime, the world economy would substantially collapse and much of the Arab Gulf region would be uninhabitable.

Finally, even if it were somehow possible to "win" militarily, renewed US aggression would be morally reprehensible and illegal in every possible way.  We're the bad guys in this one and we lost.  Deal with it.

The right thing to do is for the US to leave the Gulf and permit Iran and Oman to structure an arrangement, acceptable to the region, for transit through the Strait of Hormuz that will allow commerce to flow again.

comments.name: State College Graduate
comments.body:
Why do so many writers use the term “bracing” when describing heat waves. 

Is it because the word “wave” is in the phrase? Like when an ocean wave comes at you? 

My fellow humans in Europe: Take it from a Californian, you don’t “brace” for a heat wave! You are not in the ocean. You go out and buy an air conditioner!  If it lies dormant for 11 months of the year, then great!  Make a nice cover for it and let it lie dormant, just like your winter holiday decorations may. 

But there is no bracing for a heat wave! You either leave your hot home and spend days at a cooling center, or travel to a cooler city if you can afford that, or you buy an air conditioner.

There are portable A/Cs and window A/Cs.  There are videos online of how to install them if you can’t find someone to do that work. The portable ones are the simplest to install and store away for next year.  

Would you “brace” for the winter? Of course not. You would prepare for the longs months of winter. Now you have to prepare for the heat too. It will be back next year!

I have known Malaga since the 1960s, and my uncle was part of the management team for the reconstruction of the cities docks in the 1950s.  There was no previous golden age that has been destroyed, Old-time Malaga was dirty, gritty and hard-scrabble. Pickpocketing and petty crime was rife - those rejas were not just cute window adornments.

I was back in Malaga last Fall and truly the city has been transformed in just about everyway for the good. Its major asset is its historic core, and pretty reasonably it is exploiting that for the tens of millions of euros that it generates for the workers who now have jobs and real careers available to them. Does that mean that there has been some disruption to the old ways? Of course, but it is vastly for the better for nearly everybody.

Integral to these changes of the very small historic core has been a large investment in public transport, with light rail and new roads enabling people to live in easy commuting distance of the previously (frankly) often squalid center. New housing, with modern amenities make life immeasurably better for most people.

Malaga, under this mayor, has also got on top of the old problems of corruption and chicanery that would make a New Yorker blush. Nowhere is perfect, but being able to run a business without having to pay-off multiple tiers of villainy is a great achievement.

As always, you can escape 'mass tourism' by walking a couple of blocks.

x86 is public and technically anyone could build a simple chip. Intel & AMD have cross-licensing agreements on Intel's extensions like MMX & SSE along with AMD64. The extensions aren't public and it's probably impossible to build a chip without violating someone's patent.

For at least 30 years, the actual instruction set hasn't really mattered. All CPUs have a translation layer that converts their CISC (like x86) into an internal RISC architecture. As more cache and execution units get stuffed in, the translation takes up a smaller and smaller % of the transistor budget.

Most code is written in high-level languages and can be recompiled for any chip architecture. I don't trust Washington to get regulation right for an issue nobody there understands. I don't know of any engineers in Congress besides Thomas Massie and he lost his primary.

Spain: the Volunteer Astronomy Observers of Spain maintains Eclipse Seguro (Eclipse Safety), an official regional vetting initiative specifically created to list verified, safe suppliers of eclipse glasses across Europe.
Major European bodies like the Royal Astronomical Society 
(RAS-UK) or national observatories issue safety guides that redirect viewers to verified manufacturers or optics distributors.

The American Astronomical Society has “The AAS Suppliers of Safe Solar Viewers & Filters” page that includes major European and United Kingdom manufacturers. The AAS collaborates internationally and verifies that European manufacturers meet standard lab certifications.
You can bypass third-party online sellers, and buy directly from long-standing European companies and AAS-listed manufacturers in Europe.
>Bresser (Germany)
>Baader Planetarium (Germany- and famous for “Astrosolar Safety Film”)

comments.body: I've had the good fortune this year to grow my own lettuce in the backyard. I joined a seed saving group and was sent 3 different types of unique lettuce seed to try and grow. The lettuce had been outstanding and my wife and I have a large salad most days for lunch. We don't use our backyard as a toilet so the chance of getting sick is very very low. The growing season will continue up until the first frost, maybe a little after that. Before the growing season I did have my soiled tested by Brooklyn college for safety. Will do again next year.

articles.title: Worried About the Lettuce in Your Salad? Some New Yorkers Opt to Buy Local.
articles.summary: With an intestinal illness called cyclosporiasis causing concern about the produce supply, some consumers have turned to smaller, regional growers.
